name: The Grandfathered Hole in the Ground: How Landfill Scarcity Prints Above-Inflation Pricing Every Quarter
deck: No major US metro has permitted a new large landfill in about twenty years, so Republic and Waste Management raise prices faster than their costs quarter after quarter - and because their service territories barely overlap, they never have to compete with each other to do it.
core_bet: Permitted landfills are irreplaceable local monopolies. Building a new large one in a populated area takes the better part of a decade, hundreds of millions in review, and usually fails against community opposition, so the ones that exist are grandfathered assets no competitor can replicate. That lets Republic Services and Waste Management push disposal and collection pricing above cost inflation every single quarter, largely independent of volume, because households and businesses generate waste inelastically and cannot exit. The non-obvious structural fact is that the two majors do not check each other's pricing, because their service territories don't overlap - geographic non-competition delivers de facto local monopoly economics without any of the rate regulation a utility would face.

mechanism: The moat is a permit, not a machine. New landfill permitting in a populated area is close to impossible: it takes years of review, faces opposition from every adjacent community, costs hundreds of millions, and frequently fails, so no major US metropolitan area has successfully permitted a new large landfill in roughly two decades. Existing permitted landfills are grandfathered with sunk capital and local acceptance. A single large site can serve millions of people for a decade-plus, so most metros run on just one or two privately owned landfills that absorb all residual waste. Republic and Waste Management own both the collection routes and the disposal endpoint, so they move waste from route to landfill at near-zero marginal cost while any independent hauler must pay them a tipping fee that keeps rising - squeezing the independent's spread until selling out is the only exit.

The pricing shows up quarter after quarter regardless of volume. Republic delivered 50 basis points of adjusted EBITDA margin expansion in Q1 2026 explicitly from pricing in excess of cost inflation, then repeated the message in Q2 2026 ($4.43B revenue, resilient margins, pricing ahead of costs). Waste Management guided 2026 collection and disposal core price of 5.4-5.8% with yield of 3.2-3.6% - price, not volume (guided at just 0.2-0.6%), is doing the work. Casella, a regional operator with dense Northeast landfill control, posted solid-waste pricing up 5.5% in Q2 2026 (5.8% collection, 4.7% disposal) and 4.9% for full-year 2025, and management said 2025 was its fifth consecutive year of double-digit growth in revenue, adjusted EBITDA, and adjusted free cash flow. The moat works at national scale and at regional scale alike.

The spread compounds because waste is inelastic and the majors buy their way to more density. A household or business cannot meaningfully cut volume in response to a 5-6% annual increase, and inflation runs lower, so the gap between price and cost widens year after year. Republic converts this into a 32% FY2025 adjusted EBITDA margin ($5.31B on $16.59B revenue), $7.02 adjusted EPS, and $2.43B of adjusted free cash flow - fortress-level, oligopoly-style profitability. Then it compounds the advantage through acquisitions, spending over $700M in H1 2026 alone: it buys independent haulers at normalized multiples and applies its disposal-consolidation economics, eliminating redundant capacity and widening the spread on the acquired routes. Waste Management is doing the same on its side of the map, integrating Stericycle into a recurring collection-and-disposal base with FY2025 revenue of $25.204B and free cash flow of $2.937B.
why_now: The dated inflection is that pricing is now visibly detached from volume and repeating every quarter. Waste Management's own 2026 guidance, set January 28, 2026, calls for collection and disposal core price of 5.4-5.8% against volume of just 0.2-0.6% - the company is guiding to grow almost entirely on price. Republic posted 50bps of adjusted EBITDA margin expansion in Q1 2026 from pricing above cost inflation and raised full-year 2026 guidance on August 6, 2026 to $17.20-$17.30B revenue and $5.525-$5.550B adjusted EBITDA. Casella's Q2 2026 solid-waste pricing of 5.5% extended a fifth straight year of double-digit financial growth. This is not a cyclical spike: landfill scarcity is structurally worsening as communities densify and pass no-new-landfill measures, recycling rates plateau in the 30-40% range so most waste still lands in the ground, and ESG-driven investment in RNG and landfill-gas capture adds revenue on top of the same scarce permits rather than eroding them. The scarcity is entrenched for the next 15-20 years, which is exactly why the pricing power keeps printing.
who_pays: Households and businesses pay through disposal bills that rise faster than inflation every year, a burden that lands hardest on lower-income households as a share of budget and on municipalities whose waste-line costs crowd out other services. Independent haulers that don't own landfills pay through margin compression - they win routes at competitive prices but pay Republic's or WM's ever-rising tipping fees until acquisition is their only exit. Communities that try public landfills, regional cooperation, or waste-to-energy find them economically inferior to private scale and give up. The bill is universal and quietly regressive.
who_profits: Republic Services and Waste Management capture nearly all the value: Republic's 32% FY2025 adjusted EBITDA margin, $2.43B adjusted free cash flow, and 50bps-per-quarter margin expansion flow straight to shareholders, and WM's $2.937B FY2025 free cash flow does the same. Casella proves the moat scales down to a strong regional operator. The permits themselves never trade, but they sit inside the operators as embedded, near-perpetual options. Regional roll-up platforms backed by financial sponsors profit from the same scarcity applied to acquired independents - which is why Republic's and WM's own acquisition machines keep absorbing them.
tension: The threat is political and regulatory, not competitive. Because waste bills are universal and hit household budgets while operators earn 30%+ margins, elected officials and regulators increasingly resent above-inflation increases, and a move toward waste-utility rate regulation (cost-plus or capped increases) would end the pricing-power moat overnight. Demand destruction is a slower risk: genuine consumption reduction, source-side packaging mandates, or scaled chemical recycling and waste-to-energy could shrink the scarcity premium. And the majors carry real operating exposure - labor and retention, fuel, recycling-commodity swings, and PFAS-linked landfill liability. None are near-term, but all press on a moat that today looks unassailable.
surprising_part: Republic and Waste Management essentially never compete on price - because their service territories don't overlap. A household in a Republic area pays Republic's price; there is no option to switch to WM, because WM doesn't run trucks there, and vice versa. The two national 'competitors' are really a patchwork of adjacent local monopolies that price independently without needing any agreement to do so. That geographic non-competition reproduces regulated-utility economics - captive customers, guaranteed demand, above-inflation price increases - with none of the rate oversight a utility faces. The moat isn't that they beat each other; it's that they were never in the same ring.
one_sentence: A permitted landfill is a modern oil well - finite, grandfathered, and impossible to drill a new one next to - and Republic and Waste Management tax every household and business for the privilege of throwing something away, without ever having to compete with each other to set the price.
societal_stake: Above-inflation waste pricing is a slow affordability tax that compounds for years and weighs most on lower-income households, and communities have little agency to escape it: they cannot pick their operator, cannot permit their own landfill without a regulatory gauntlet, and cannot easily force meaningful recycling or circular investment from incumbents who profit more from cheap disposal than from waste reduction. Cheap landfill capacity (cheap to the operator, not the customer) also mutes the price signal that would otherwise push genuine circular-economy adoption. And the political economy is self-reinforcing: operator lobbying makes new-landfill permitting even harder, deepening the scarcity that justifies the pricing power in the first place.
